newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU moves to agree cross-border payments rules.
newsitem.headline: EU moves to agree cross-border payments rules.

text.p: The European Union will try in the coming weeks to bridge differences over draft legislation to make payment transfers within the 15-nation bloc safer, quicker and possibly cheaper.

At issue is what EU institutions see as a persistant inability by banks to voluntarily improve the service of transferring small sums of money to pay for such things as foreign magazine subscriptions or a deposit on a holiday abroad.

But while the Council of EU ministers and the European Parliament -- which share decision-making on legislation affecting the bloc's single market -- agree on the facts, they propose different solutions.

That is why representatives of the two institutions and the European Commission will start a so-called conciliation committee meeting on October 10 on the draft directive on credit transfers, EU sources said on Tuesday.
Under EU rules, the committee must reach a compromise within six weeks of meeting.

In November 1994 -- following long-standing complaints from consumer organisations -- the Commission proposed banks should execute cross-border payment orders within six working days, avoid charging both the sender and the receiver of the money for the service and be made liable for lost transfers.
EU finance ministers agreed in December 1995 that the draft directive should cover payments below 25,000 European currency units ($31,250) to be increased to 30,000 Ecus after two years.
But the parliament wants the minimum coverage to be 50,000 Ecus, arguing the need to protect small businesses as well as individuals.
Ireland, which took over the six-month rotating EU presidency in July, is aiming to get a deal at 35,000 Ecus from the date of entry into force of the directive, a diplomat said.
But just when this happens is another point of contention between EU ministers and the parliament.

EU sources said the most likely compromise was for the directive -- which must be transposed into national laws -- to come into force at the same time as the introduction of a single European currency in January, 1 1999.

The most difficult issue remains, however, the level of banks' liability for lost transfers. EU ministers agreed banks should be obliged to refund a minimum of 10,000 Ecus only, due to fears a higher amount would have a prejudicial effect on credit institution's solvency requirements.
But the parliament wants to double this.
An attempt by the Irish presidency to find a compromise at 15,000 Ecus met with the stiff opposition of France, Germany, Belgium, Austria and the Netherlands, a Commission source said.
European banks have criticised the plan saying small value cross-border transfers cost them a lot of money because they usually involve several banks and a lot of paper work.

But European commissioner in charge of the EU's single market Mario Monti argues that European citizens and small businesses, not only banks which can operate freely in the bloc, must also see the benefits of a borderless Union. ($1 = 0.80 Ecus)
